concept.body: Fingerprint chart, one pair at a time: x-only flipped → y-axis mirror. y-only flipped → x-axis mirror. Both flipped → 180° turn. Swapped → y = x mirror. Same nonzero amounts ADDED to all points → translation. Match the pattern, then re-check it on a second point.

explanationVariants: (6, 2) → (6, −2): x kept, y negated — the x-axis mirror.
Only the coordinate measuring height flipped, so the mirror is the horizontal axis.

widget.prompt: Two points move: (6, 2) → (6, −2) and (1, 5) → (1, −5). Which motion fits?

options.label: reflection over the x-axis
options.feedback: Both points: y flipped, x untouched — the x-axis mirror's fingerprint, confirmed twice.

options.label: reflection over the y-axis
options.feedback: That mirror flips the X: (6, 2) would go to (−6, 2). Here both x's survived.

options.label: a 180° rotation
options.feedback: The half turn flips BOTH: (6, 2) would land at (−6, −2), but the x stayed positive.

options.label: a translation
options.feedback: A slide moves every point by the SAME vector — but the first point dropped 4 while the second dropped 10. Unequal shifts rule out any translation.

steps.body: Detective work: given both figures' coordinates, identify the motion. **Compare a preimage point with its image and read the pattern**: both coordinates shifted by constants → translation. Signs flipped or coordinates swapped → reflection or rotation. Then CONFIRM the candidate on every remaining point — one point can lie, three can't.
Detective work with a live suspect: recover the motion from the coordinates.

widget.prompt: ΔABC has A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 3); the dashed image is ΔDEF. Recover the motion that maps one onto the other.
widget.successFeedback: (x, y) → (x + 2, y + 4): the shift read off A → D moved B and C onto E and F too — one rule, every point.
widget.offsetFeedback: The shape matches but the shift is off. Read it from a single pair: A(1, 1) → D(3, 5) means dx = 3 − 1 = 2 and dy = 5 − 1 = 4.
widget.reflectFeedback: A flip reverses the triangle's orientation — but ΔDEF winds the same way as ΔABC, so no reflection is involved. Turn it off and slide only.

predict.prompt: A(1, 1) maps to D(3, 5). To land B and C on their images too, each must move by…

options.label: The same (dx, dy) — one rule moves every point
Its own amount — corners can travel differently

predict.reveal: A translation is one rule for the whole plane: every point slides by the same (dx, dy). Reading A → D gives (+2, +4) — and B and C must obey the identical shift, or the motion was never a translation at all.

cml.actionGoal: Transform a figure and observe which coordinates and geometric properties change or remain invariant.

explanationVariants: The identified motion applies to EVERY point of the figure: (2, 2) → (2 + 2, 2 + 4) = (4, 6), so the x-coordinate is 4.
Once the motion is named, any new point rides the same rule — add 2 to x.

widget.prompt: Using the translation (x, y) → (x + 2, y + 4) from the last problem: point (2, 2) lies inside ΔABC. What is the x-coordinate of its image?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is 2 + 4 — the y-shift applied to x. Keep each shift in its own slot: x gets +2, so 2 + 2 = 4.
2 is unmoved — but the motion carries EVERY point of the figure, interior included: 2 + 2 = 4.

steps.body: **Sign patterns are fingerprints.** Only x flips: reflection over the y-axis. Only y flips: reflection over the x-axis. BOTH flip: 180° rotation. Coordinates swap: the y = x mirror. Read the pattern off one pair, then verify it on the rest.

widget.prompt: A(2, 3) and B(5, 1) map to A′(−2, 3) and B′(−5, 1). Which motion is it?

options.label: reflection over the y-axis
options.feedback: Both points: x negated, y untouched — the y-axis mirror's exact fingerprint, confirmed twice.

options.label: reflection over the x-axis
options.feedback: The x-axis mirror flips the Y: A would go to (2, −3). Here the y's survived and the x's flipped — other mirror.

options.label: a 180° rotation about the origin
options.feedback: The half turn flips BOTH signs: A would land at (−2, −3), but A′ keeps y = 3.

options.label: a translation
options.feedback: A slide shifts both points by the SAME amounts — but A moved 4 left while B moved 10 left. Unequal shifts rule out any translation.

explanationVariants: A(1,4) → (−1,−4) and B(3,1) → (−3,−1): both coordinates negated on both points — the 180° rotation's fingerprint.
Test the alternative mirrors: the y-axis would keep y = 4; the x-axis would keep x = 1. Only the half turn flips everything.

widget.prompt: A(1, 4) and B(3, 1) map to A′(−1, −4) and B′(−3, −1). Which motion is it?

options.label: a 180° rotation about the origin
options.feedback: Both signs of both points flipped, order intact — exactly (x, y) → (−x, −y).

options.label: reflection over the y-axis
options.feedback: That mirror flips only x: A would land at (−1, 4), but A′ has y = −4 too.

options.label: reflection over the x-axis
options.feedback: That mirror flips only y: A would land at (1, −4), but A′'s x also flipped to −1.

options.label: reflection over the line y = x
options.feedback: The swap sends A(1,4) to (4,1) — no sign changes at all. These images are fully negated instead.

steps.body: Sometimes the detective's answer is **no motion exists**. Rigid motions preserve distance, so if ANY pair of matched points sits at a different distance than its partners, no slide, turn, flip, or chain can ever connect the figures. Measure first; it can end the case immediately.

widget.prompt: C is at (2, 1) and D is at (2, 7). What is the length CD?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is 7 + 1 — coordinates added. Length along a vertical segment is the DIFFERENCE of the y's: 7 − 1 = 6.
9 is 2 + 7 — an x mixed with a y. Both points share x = 2; only the y's differ: 7 − 1 = 6.

hints: Compare the two lengths before hunting for a motion.
AB = 5 and CD = 6 (just measured). What must a rigid motion do to lengths?
A motion mapping AB onto CD would have to stretch 5 into 6 — can any rigid motion do that?
explanationVariants: AB = 5 but CD = 6. Rigid motions preserve distance, so mapping AB onto CD would require a stretch — impossible. No rigid motion exists; the segments are not congruent.
Congruence fails the moment one measurement disagrees: 5 ≠ 6 closes the case before any motion is tried.

widget.prompt: A(0, 0), B(5, 0) — so AB = 5. C(2, 1), D(2, 7) — so CD = 6. Is there a rigid motion mapping segment AB onto segment CD?

options.label: No — the lengths differ (5 vs 6), and rigid motions preserve length
options.feedback: One mismatched distance is a complete proof of impossibility: rigid motions never stretch.

options.label: Yes — translate A to C, then rotate B around to D
options.feedback: The rotation swings B on a radius-5 circle around C — and D sits 6 away, off that circle. The endpoint can never land.

options.label: Yes — a 90° rotation turns horizontal segments into vertical ones
options.feedback: It fixes the DIRECTION mismatch but not the length: the rotated segment is still 5 long, one unit short of CD.

options.label: It cannot be decided from coordinates alone
options.feedback: Coordinates decide it completely — they give exact lengths (5 and 6), and unequal lengths forbid any rigid motion.

steps.body: Name the motion — or refute it.
takeaways: Read the pattern: constant shifts = translation; sign flips/swaps = mirrors and turns.
Confirm the candidate on EVERY point — one point can lie.
Unequal distances end the case: no rigid motion, no congruence.
